## Summary {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| echo: false
Markdown(f"""
**Expected goals (xG)** is the probability that an average player scores a given chance. I built an xG
model from every shot in StatsBomb's free event data ({len(shots):,} shots from
{shots['match_id'].nunique():,} men's and women's matches) and used it to ask how much of "great finishing"
is skill.

- **The model is competitive with a professional one.** On {comparison['test_matches']} held-out matches it
  scores a log loss of {ours.log_loss:.4f} against {sb.log_loss:.4f} for StatsBomb's own xG (ROC AUC
  {ours.roc_auc:.3f} vs {sb.roc_auc:.3f}). Most of the gain is on women's matches.
- **Where the goalkeeper stands matters more than the shot angle.** The freeze frame (every player's
  position at the moment of the shot) carries most of the signal.
- **A men's model works for women's football.** Trained only on men's shots, it is well calibrated on
  women's matches.
- **For almost every player, beating xG is luck.** Over-performance in one half of a player's matches
  barely predicts the other half (r = {p_all['split_half_r']:.2f}, {p_all['players']} players).
- **Messi is the exception.** Even measured against his Barcelona team-mates, who also beat xG, he scored
  {messi.goals_above_team_adjusted:.0f} more non-penalty goals than expected, about
  {messi.goals_above_team_adjusted / ((messi.luck_high - messi.luck_low) / 2):.1f} times the range luck allows.
""")
```

## Data

[StatsBomb Open Data](https://github.com/statsbomb/open-data) publishes full event data for selected
competitions: every shot with its location, body part and technique, the pass that set it up, and a
**freeze frame** (the position of every visible player when the ball was struck).
Penalty shoot-outs are excluded.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-coverage
#| tbl-cap: "Shots by gender. The open data favours some teams and tournaments (Barcelona 2004–2021, World Cups, Euros), so it is not a random sample of football."
coverage = (shots.groupby("gender", observed=True)
            .agg(matches=("match_id", "nunique"), shots=("shot_id", "size"), goals=("is_goal", "sum"),
                 competitions=("competition", "nunique"))
            .rename(index={"female": "Women", "male": "Men"}))
coverage["goals per shot"] = (coverage["goals"] / coverage["shots"]).round(3)
coverage
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-freeze-frame
#| fig-cap: "One shot and its freeze frame. The shaded triangle is the shooting cone from the ball to the posts; anyone inside it can block the shot."
example = shots[(shots["is_goal"] == 1) & shots["freeze_frame"].notna() & shots["xg"].between(0.25, 0.35)].iloc[0]
frame = np.array(json.loads(example["freeze_frame"]))
pitch, fig, ax = shared.half_pitch(figsize=(6, 4.4), x_min=78)
pitch.polygon([[(example.x, example.y), (120, 36), (120, 44)]], ax=ax, color=shared.OURS_COLOUR, alpha=0.15)
for is_mate, is_gk, colour, marker in [(0, 0, "#264653", "o"), (1, 0, "#7fb7be", "o"), (0, 1, "#2a9d8f", "s")]:
    sel = frame[(frame[:, 2] == is_mate) & (frame[:, 3] == is_gk)]
    if len(sel):
        pitch.scatter(sel[:, 0], sel[:, 1], ax=ax, s=120, color=colour, marker=marker, edgecolors="white")
pitch.scatter([example.x], [example.y], ax=ax, s=200, color=shared.GOAL_COLOUR, edgecolors="white")
ax.set_title(f"{example.player}, {example.home_team} v {example.away_team} ({example.match_date}): "
             f"xG {example.xg:.2f}", fontsize=9)
plt.show()
```

## Features and model

`features.shot_features()` builds every feature. The training script, the evaluation and the app's
simulator all call it, so a shot placed in the app is scored exactly like a real one.

- **Geometry:** distance to goal, the angle the goal mouth subtends, how wide the shot is.
- **Freeze frame:** defenders and team-mates in the shooting cone; the nearest defender and how many are
  within 3 and 5 yards; the keeper's distance from goal and from the shooter, how far the keeper has
  come out, and how far he is off the line of the shot.
- **Context:** body part, technique, first-time, one-on-one, under pressure, phase of play, and the
  assist (cross, cut-back, through ball, its height and length).

The model is LightGBM, with the number of trees chosen by 5-fold cross-validation grouped by match (shots
from one match never sit on both sides of a split). Penalties get a constant: the training conversion
rate, `{python} f"{model.penalty_xg:.3f}"`.

### Two fixes found by using the model

Building the simulator exposed two flaws that the test metrics could not see:

1. **Wide shots looked better than central ones.** The first model gave a shot from the touchline 25
   yards out *more* xG than a central one at the same distance. About 35 freak goals from wide areas
   (mishit crosses) had pulled the trees. **Monotonic constraints** fixed it: xG must fall with distance,
   width and defenders in the cone, and rise with the angle.
2. **"Keeper far away" meant "easy goal".** In real data a keeper 40 yards from the shooter is usually
   one who has left his goal, so the model rewarded large distances. That fired wrongly for any long or
   wide shot with the keeper on his line. The distance is now **capped at 12 yards**, with a separate
   "keeper advance" feature (how far he has come out towards the shooter) carrying the real signal.

Both changes cost almost nothing in held-out log loss (about +0.0003) and make the model behave
sensibly everywhere on the pitch.

```{python}
#| label: fig-xg-map
#| fig-cap: "xG from every spot: an unpressured right-foot shot with the keeper in position and no defenders."
grid = scene.xg_grid(model, step=1.0, x_min=78.0)
xs, ys = np.sort(grid["x"].unique()), np.sort(grid["y"].unique())
values = grid.pivot(index="x", columns="y", values="xg").loc[xs, ys].to_numpy()
pitch, fig, ax = shared.half_pitch(figsize=(6, 4.4), x_min=78)
ylim, xlim = ax.get_ylim(), ax.get_xlim()
im = ax.imshow(values, origin="lower", extent=[0, 80, 78, 120], cmap="YlOrRd", alpha=0.75, vmin=0, vmax=0.6,
               interpolation="bilinear", aspect="auto", zorder=1)
ax.set_xlim(xlim)
ax.set_ylim(ylim)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.7, label="xG")
plt.show()
```

## How good is it?

Twenty percent of matches, chosen within every competition-season, were held out before any modelling.
@tbl-metrics scores three models on their non-penalty shots: the textbook distance-and-angle logistic
regression, this project's model, and **StatsBomb's own xG**, which ships with the data.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-metrics
#| tbl-cap: "Held-out non-penalty shots. Log loss and Brier: lower is better. ROC AUC: how well the model ranks goals above misses. Calibration error: shot-weighted gap between xG and the actual goal rate."
np_metrics[["log_loss", "brier", "roc_auc", "ece", "goals", "xg"]].rename(columns={
    "log_loss": "Log loss", "brier": "Brier", "roc_auc": "ROC AUC", "ece": "Calibration error",
    "goals": "Goals", "xg": "Total xG"}).round({"Log loss": 4, "Brier": 4, "ROC AUC": 3,
                                                 "Calibration error": 4, "Total xG": 0})
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Calibration on held-out shots. StatsBomb's values run slightly low on this data."
test = shots[shots["xg_holdout"].notna() & (shots["shot_type"] != "Penalty")]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4.4))
for name, col, colour in [("This project", "xg_holdout", shared.OURS_COLOUR),
                          ("StatsBomb", "statsbomb_xg", shared.SB_COLOUR)]:
    b = shared.calibration_bins(test["is_goal"].to_numpy(), test[col].to_numpy(float))
    ax.plot(b["mean_xg"], b["goal_rate"], "o-", color=colour, label=name)
ax.plot([0, 0.7], [0, 0.7], "--", color="#999", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("Predicted xG")
ax.set_ylabel("Share scored")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
Markdown(f"""
**Is the comparison fair?** Not entirely, and the biases run both ways. StatsBomb's model is
built on far more data than is public and may well have seen these very matches; but it was not tuned to
these competitions, and this model was. Part of a log-loss edge can come from calibration alone (StatsBomb's
values add up to {sb.xg:,.0f} goals where {int(sb.goals):,} were scored). So I re-calibrated StatsBomb's
values on the training matches (Platt scaling, separately by gender) and compared again: this model is still
ahead by **{-comparison['difference']:.4f}** in log loss (95% CI {-comparison['ci_high']:.4f} to
{-comparison['ci_low']:.4f}, bootstrapping the {comparison['test_matches']} test matches). ROC AUC, which
ignores calibration altogether, tells the same story. The edge is real but small. The fair summary is
*"on par with StatsBomb on men's football, slightly better on women's"*, not "better than StatsBomb".
""")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-importance
#| fig-cap: "Share of the model's total gain by feature. Grouped, the keeper's position carries 45% and the whole freeze frame 56%, against 25% for distance and angle together."
gain = pd.Series(model.booster.feature_importance("gain"), model.booster.feature_name())
gain = (gain / gain.sum()).sort_values().tail(12)
from pages_src.simulator import FEATURE_LABELS
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.2))
ax.barh([FEATURE_LABELS.get(f, f) for f in gain.index], gain.values, color=shared.OURS_COLOUR)
ax.set_xlabel("Share of total gain")
plt.show()
```

Markdown(f"""
A model that has **never seen a women's match** predicts {row.xg:.0f} goals on the women's test matches,

## Is finishing a skill?

All numbers here use **out-of-fold xG**: every shot is scored by a model that never saw its match, so a
player cannot "beat" a model fitted to their own shots.

### Luck is large

Even an average finisher drifts above or below xG. Simulating each shot as a coin flip with probability
equal to its xG gives the range luck alone produces for the *same* chances (@fig-funnel).

```{python}
#| label: fig-funnel
#| fig-cap: "Goals minus xG for every player with at least 150 non-penalty shots. Grey: 95% range of luck alone."
order = finishing.sort_values("xg")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.4))
ax.fill_between(order["xg"], order["luck_low"], order["luck_high"], color="#ddd", step="mid",
                label="Luck alone (95%)")
inside = ~finishing["beyond_luck"]
ax.scatter(finishing.loc[inside, "xg"], finishing.loc[inside, "goals_minus_xg"], s=22, color=shared.MISS_COLOUR)
ax.scatter(finishing.loc[~inside, "xg"], finishing.loc[~inside, "goals_minus_xg"], s=36, color=shared.GOAL_COLOUR,
           label="Beyond luck")
for _, r in finishing[~inside].iterrows():
    ax.annotate("Messi" if r["player"] == shared.MESSI else r["player"].split()[0],
                (r["xg"], r["goals_minus_xg"]), xytext=(4, 3), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8)
ax.axhline(0, color="#444", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("Total xG (log scale)")
ax.set_ylabel("Goals − xG")
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left")
plt.show()
```

### Hot streaks don't repeat

```{python}
#| echo: false
male, female = persistence["male"], persistence["female"]
Markdown(f"""
If finishing were a strong skill, a player who beats xG in half their matches would beat it in the other
half too. Splitting each player's matches into alternating halves (at least
{p_all['min_shots_per_half']} shots in each), the correlation of per-shot goals-minus-xG between halves is
**r = {p_all['split_half_r']:.2f}** (95% CI {p_all['ci_low']:.2f} to {p_all['ci_high']:.2f};
{p_all['players']} players): {male['split_half_r']:.2f} for men, {female['split_half_r']:.2f} for women. For a
typical player, a season of hot finishing says almost nothing about the next. That doesn't mean finishing
skill is zero, only that with a few dozen shots per half it is too small to tell apart from luck.
""")
```

### …except Messi

```{python}
#| label: tbl-messi
#| tbl-cap: "Non-penalty goals vs out-of-fold xG. Luck: the 95% range of goals − xG for an average finisher on the same shots."
messi_team.assign(**{"goals − xG": messi_team["goals"] - messi_team["xg"]})[
    ["group", "shots", "goals", "xg", "goals − xG", "luck_low", "luck_high"]].round(1)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
Markdown(f"""
Messi scored **{int(messi.goals)}** non-penalty goals for Barcelona from **{messi.xg:.0f}** xG. But his
team-mates *also* beat xG, by {mates.goals_per_xg - 1:.0%}, more than luck allows. Part of the gap is
therefore a team effect the model cannot see: the quality of chances Barcelona created, which a freeze
frame only partly captures. Scaling Messi's xG by his team-mates' rate still leaves
**+{messi.goals_above_team_adjusted:.0f} goals**, against a luck range of about
±{(messi.luck_high - messi.luck_low) / 2:.0f}. Away from Barcelona (Argentina, PSG, Inter Miami; only
{int(messi_team.iloc[2].shots)} shots) his finishing is within luck.
""")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-messi-seasons
#| fig-cap: "Messi's goals − xG by competition-season (≥ 30 shots). Whiskers: 95% luck range; red bars are beyond it."
s = messi_seasons[messi_seasons["shots"] >= 30].reset_index(drop=True)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
colours = [shared.GOAL_COLOUR if g > h else shared.MISS_COLOUR for g, h in zip(s["goals_minus_xg"], s["luck_high"])]
ax.bar(s.index, s["goals_minus_xg"], color=colours)
ax.errorbar(s.index, np.zeros(len(s)), yerr=[-s["luck_low"], s["luck_high"]], fmt="none", ecolor="#999",
            capsize=3, lw=1)
ax.set_xticks(s.index, [f"{a}\n{b.replace('La Liga', '').strip()}" for a, b in zip(s["season"], s["competition"])],
              fontsize=7)
ax.axhline(0, color="#444", lw=0.8)
ax.set_ylabel("Goals − xG")
plt.show()
```

## Limitations

- **Not a random sample.** The open data covers Barcelona's 2004–2021 seasons in full, several complete
  2015/16 leagues, and many tournaments. Findings describe these matches.
- **What xG can't see.** Freeze frames give positions, not the ball's spin, the shooter's balance, or
  which is their stronger foot. Some of what looks like finishing skill is information the model lacks.
- **Team effects.** As Barcelona shows, a team can systematically create better chances than its freeze
  frames suggest. Player-level finishing should be judged against team-mates, not just the model.
- **The StatsBomb comparison** is informative, not a head-to-head contest: the two models were built for
  different purposes on different data.
